To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Appalachian Piedmont is a tectonite belt in which recrystallizing and recrystalled quartz is abundant, and that the nontectonic rocks of the Valley and Ridge are transitional to the tectonics of the Piedmont in a belt which trends northeast-southwest across the Valley and Ridge, and that this transitional belt is the locus of the greatest amount of penetrative deformation.
the lower limit of visible recrystallizaton and flowage in quartzite is a function of the intensity of deformation.

recrystallizing SiO 2 is the most important agent of flowage in the Appalachian quartzites, the degree of deformation increases toward the southeast, and the limits of visible recrystallizaion and flowage are gradational and are not sharp boundaries.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the definition of the lower limits of visible deformation; (2) the determination of the limits of visible flowage; (3) the determination of recrystalli-zation in the central Appalachia; and (4) the establishment of the limits of the Appalachian Piedmont and the definition of the transitional zone.
a detailed study of the deformational history and structural evolution of the crystalline rocks in a portion of the central Appalachians.
the development of a quantitative method for the recognition of deformation fabrics in quartz-rich rocks, and with the application of the method to the study of Appalachian geology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Appalachian quartzite is tectonic in the southeastern and central areas, and nontectonic in the northwestern and western parts.
the Appalachian Piedmont is a zone of deformation which is transitional from a tectonically stable area on the northwest to an area of intense deformation on the southeast.
the rocks of the Appalachian Piedmont have not been deformed since the early Paleozoic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Appalachian tectonites are the result of a single episode of penetrative movement.
recrystallisation is a function of the degree of deformation, and the degree of deformation is a function of distance from the crystalline axis of the Appalachians.
the rocks of the Appalachian Piedmont are tectonites.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Appalachian Piedmont is not an impenetrable barrier to the study of Appalachian geology.
recrystallisation and flowage are the most important processes in the deformation of quartz-rich rocks and that the limits of deformation can be defined in terms of recrystallsied quartz.
the deformation of quartz-rich rock in the central Appalachias is continuous and gradual, and that the limits of deformation can be determined by careful analysis of the fabric of quartz.
